items.learnMore:
Recognizing the shape

Most real-world complexity classes map to a recognizable code shape: direct index access is O(1); a single loop over the input is O(n); halving a search space each step is O(log n); a loop nested inside a loop over the same collection is O(n²).

Common mistake

Assuming 'sorted' automatically means O(log n) lookups — only true if the code actually uses a search that exploits the sort, like binary search.

Why constants get dropped

Big-O cares about the LIMITING behavior as n grows without bound. A constant multiplier (3n vs n) changes the exact runtime but not the fundamental shape of the curve — both are straight lines, just with different slopes. Common mistake

items.prompt: What real-world code pattern most commonly produces O(n²) complexity by accident?
choices: A single loop that reads each item exactly once and does nothing else inside it
A loop where each iteration performs an operation (like a membership check or a search) that itself scans the whole collection
A function with a very long chain of if/else statements checking many conditions

items.explanation: A loop of n iterations where each iteration does O(n) work (like scanning an array for membership) multiplies to O(n²) — this is exactly the shape of the unit's incident, disguised as a single innocent-looking check.
items.reference:
for record in records: # n times
  if record.id not in result: # scans up to n items

Why: n outer iterations × up to n inner scan work = O(n²) — no visible nested `for` keyword required.

Worst-case behavior can only happen if the Set stores objects, never primitive values
items.explanation: Average-case guarantees assume typical, non-adversarial data — if an attacker can choose the input, they can potentially choose values engineered to trigger the rare worst case deliberately, which is exactly why the distinction isn't just academic.

items.prompt: A whitepaper claims an algorithm is 'O(1) lookup, guaranteed.' What question should you ask before trusting that claim for a security-sensitive system?
choices: Nothing — 'guaranteed' claims never need further scrutiny
Whether 'guaranteed' means worst-case or just typical/average-case performance, since the two can differ substantially
Whether the whitepaper was published in the last 12 months
Whether the algorithm is implemented in a compiled language
items.explanation: 'Guaranteed O(1)' is ambiguous unless it specifies which case it's describing — a claim that's actually about average-case performance can still have a much worse worst case that matters a great deal for adversarial or security-critical contexts.

items.prompt: For an internal batch job processing your own company's ordinary, non-adversarial data, is relying on a Set's average-case O(1) lookup generally a reasonable choice?
choices: No — average-case claims should never be trusted under any circumstances
Yes — for ordinary, non-adversarial data, the rare pathological collision case is unlikely, making the average-case claim the practically right one to rely on
Only if the batch job runs on a weekend
No, because average-case claims only apply to sorted arrays, not Sets
items.explanation: For everyday, non-adversarial data, pathological hash collisions are rare — relying on the average-case O(1) claim is the practical, reasonable choice; the worst case matters most when input could be adversarial or when a rare failure would be very costly.

items.prompt: Which of these claims is the most precise way to describe a Set's typical membership-check performance?
choices: 'Always exactly O(1), no exceptions, under any possible input'
'O(1) on average for ordinary data; can degrade toward O(n) under pathological hash collisions'
'O(n) always, regardless of the data structure used'
'Undefined — Set performance cannot be characterized at all'
items.explanation: The precise, honest claim names both halves: the typical (average) behavior and the known, rare condition (collisions) under which that typical behavior can break down.

items.prompt: Why is 'Big-O almost always describes a specific case (best, worst, or average)' an important thing to keep in mind when reading someone else's complexity claim?
choices: Because it isn't actually true — Big-O only ever describes one universal case
Because conflating which case is being described (assuming 'O(1)' always means worst-case, for example) can lead to false confidence that breaks down under real or adversarial conditions
Because Big-O claims change depending on which programming language is used
Because only senior engineers are allowed to make Big-O claims
items.explanation: A Big-O claim without a stated case is ambiguous — treating an average-case claim as if it were a worst-case guarantee is exactly the kind of mismatch that produces a 'but it said O(1)' surprise when reality doesn't match expectations.

items.prompt: A teammate swaps an array for a Set and says, 'this function is now guaranteed O(n), no matter what.' What's the most accurate correction to that statement?
choices: The correction is unnecessary — the statement is already fully accurate
It should be 'O(n) on average, for ordinary data' — the Set's O(1) lookups are an average-case property, not a worst-case guarantee
It should instead say the function is now guaranteed O(1), not O(n)
It should say the function is now guaranteed O(log n), since Sets use a tree internally
items.explanation: The honest version of the claim keeps the 'on average' qualifier — the typical case genuinely improved to O(n), but calling it an unconditional guarantee overstates what a Set's average-case O(1) lookup actually promises.

items.prompt: Implement `hasDuplicate(ids)` — given an array of ids, return `true` if any id appears more than once, `false` otherwise. Use a `Set` so the check stays O(n), not O(n²).
items.explanation: A Set gives an O(1) average-case membership check per item, so scanning n ids and checking each against the Set stays O(n) overall, instead of scanning an array for each item (which would be O(n²)).

items.prompt: Implement `countUnique(ids)` — return the number of distinct values in the `ids` array, using a `Set` to avoid an O(n²) comparison between every pair.
items.explanation: Building a Set from the array automatically collapses duplicates, since a Set only ever stores one copy of each distinct value — its `.size` is then exactly the count of unique values, computed in O(n) rather than comparing every pair.

items.prompt: Implement `firstRepeated(ids)` — return the first id (in order) that has already appeared earlier in the array, or `null` if there is no repeat. Use a `Set` to track what's been seen, keeping the check O(1) per item.
items.explanation: Scanning once while checking each id against a Set (O(1) average per check) finds the first repeat in O(n) total — the same 'scan once, check against a Set' shape as the unit's dedup fix.

items.prompt: Implement `onlyInFirst(listA, listB)` — both are arrays of plain ids (numbers or strings). Return the items from `listA` that do NOT appear anywhere in `listB`, using a Set built from `listB` to keep each check O(1).
items.explanation: Building a Set from listB once (O(m)) and then checking every item in listA against it (O(1) each) keeps the whole operation O(n + m), the same 'build a Set from one side, scan the other' pattern as `intersectionFast`.

items.prompt: Implement `mergeUnique(listA, listB)` — both are arrays of ids. Return a single array containing every distinct id from both lists, with no duplicates, using a Set to avoid an O(n²) all-pairs comparison.
items.explanation: Combining both arrays and feeding the result into a Set collapses every duplicate in one O(n + m) pass, instead of checking every item in one list against every item in the other, which would be O(n × m).

items.prompt: Implement `removeAll(ids, toRemove)` — given an array `ids` and an array `toRemove`, return `ids` with every id that also appears in `toRemove` filtered out. Use a Set built from `toRemove` for an O(1) check per item.
items.explanation: Building a Set from the (usually smaller) `toRemove` list once, then filtering `ids` against it with O(1) checks, is the exact 'build once, scan once' structure that replaced the original dedup function's nested scan.

items.prompt: Implement `appearsInBoth(listA, listB)` — return `true` if at least one id appears in both arrays, `false` otherwise. Build a Set from the smaller list for efficiency, and stop as soon as a match is found.
items.explanation: Building the Set from the smaller list keeps the one-time setup cost as low as possible, while the overall shape — build a Set once, then check membership for the rest — is the same fix idea as `intersectionFast`, just stopping early via `.some()`.

items.prompt: Implement `tagDuplicates(ids)` — return a new array of the same length as `ids`, where each entry is `true` if that id has appeared earlier in the array already, or `false` if it's the first occurrence. Use a Set to track what's been seen so far.
items.explanation: This is the dedup fix's exact loop shape (scan once, check-then-add against a Set) applied to tagging instead of filtering — each check and insert stays O(1) average-case, keeping the whole pass O(n).

items.prompt: Implement `triangularNumber(n)` — return `0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1)`, the total comparisons an array-scan dedup does in the worst case (all-unique input), using the closed-form formula rather than an actual loop.
items.explanation: The sum 0+1+...+(n-1) has the closed form n(n-1)/2 — it's the exact quadratic-shaped total the unit's array-scan dedup does in its worst case, which is why that version is O(n²).

items.prompt: Implement `linearWork(n)` — return the amount of work a simple O(n) single pass does for an input of size n (just `n` itself).
items.explanation: O(n) work is, by definition, proportional to n — the simplest model of that is just n itself, which is exactly what a single pass over every item costs.

items.prompt: Implement `quadraticWork(n)` — return `n * n`, the amount of work a naive nested-scan approach does for an input of size n.
items.explanation: n × n models the O(n²) shape directly — n outer iterations, each costing up to n — which is the exact quantity that explodes from 40,000 at n=200 to 250 billion at n=500,000 in the unit's incident.

items.prompt: Implement `growthRatio(n, multiplier)` — return how many times larger `quadraticWork` becomes when n is multiplied by `multiplier`, i.e. `(n*multiplier)^2 / n^2`, which should simplify to `multiplier^2`.
items.explanation: For an O(n²) function, multiplying n by some factor multiplies the work by that factor SQUARED — this is exactly why quadrupling the input in the unit's benchmark predicted a 16x slowdown (4² = 16), not a 4x one.

items.prompt: Implement `workAtSizes(sizes, complexityClass)` — given an array of input sizes and a complexity class (`'linear'` or `'quadratic'`), return an array of the work value at each size (n for linear, n*n for quadratic).
items.explanation: Mapping each size through the right growth formula reproduces the same table the unit's complexity-classes comparison relies on — the point isn't the code, it's seeing the two columns pull apart as n grows.

items.prompt: Implement `isFasterAt(n, complexityClassA, complexityClassB)` — given an n and two complexity classes (`'linear'` or `'quadratic'`), return `true` if class A does strictly less work than class B at that n.

tests.description: linear faster than quadratic at n=10

items.explanation: This computes the same two growth formulas and compares them directly at a given n — a small, concrete way to confirm that linear strictly beats quadratic work for any n greater than 1.

items.prompt: Implement `predictedSlowdown(multiplier)` — for a quadratic function, return the predicted slowdown factor when the input size is multiplied by `multiplier` (i.e. `multiplier * multiplier`).
items.explanation: This is the exact prediction the unit's benchmark section asks the reader to make before looking at the measured numbers — a quadratic function's slowdown is the square of however much the input grew.

items.prompt: Implement `workGap(n)` — return how many MORE units of work an O(n²) function does than an O(n) function at the same input size n (i.e. `n*n - n`).
items.explanation: At n=1 the gap is zero (both do 1 unit), but the gap grows without bound as n increases — a direct, numeric way to see why the two curves look nearly identical at small n and wildly different at large n.

items.prompt: Implement `looksQuadratic(hasOuterLoop, innerCostGrowsWithN)` — return `true` if there's an outer loop AND the inner operation's cost grows with n (the two conditions that combine to produce O(n²)).

tests.description: inner cost is constant -> not quadratic

items.explanation: This is the structural signature from L2: a loop alone isn't enough, and a growing inner cost alone isn't enough either — it's the COMBINATION of an outer loop and an inner cost that scales with n that multiplies into O(n²).

items.prompt: Implement `classifyLookup(dataStructure)` — given `'array'` or `'set'`, return `'O(n)'` for array (a scan) or `'O(1)'` for set (a hash lookup).
items.explanation: This mirrors the unit's central fact: the membership-check cost depends entirely on which data structure backs it — an array scans (O(n)), a Set hashes and jumps (O(1) average).

items.prompt: Implement `combinedComplexity(outerCount, innerComplexity)` — given the outer loop's iteration count class (`'n'` or `'1'`) and the inner operation's complexity (`'n'` or `'1'`), return the multiplied result as a string: `'O(n^2)'`, `'O(n)'`, or `'O(1)'`.
items.explanation: This directly encodes the multiplication rule from L2's derivation rules: n × n gives n², n × 1 (or 1 × n) gives n, and 1 × 1 gives a constant.

items.prompt: Implement `isSafeToRetryBlindly(method)` — given an HTTP-style method string (`'GET'`, `'PUT'`, `'DELETE'`, `'POST'`), return `true` only for the idempotent-by-convention methods (GET, PUT, DELETE), mirroring how a classifier might flag which operations are 'safe to repeat.'
items.explanation: This is a simple classification exercise in the same spirit as `detectHiddenQuadratic` and `classifyGrowth` — turning a known convention (which methods are idempotent) into a direct, checkable rule.

items.prompt: Implement `simplifyBigO(rawTerms)` — given an array of term strings like `['n^2', 'n', '1']`, return the single dominant term (the one that would survive Big-O simplification): prefer `'n^2'` over `'n'` over `'1'` if present.
items.explanation: This encodes the 'drop lower-order terms' rule directly: among a set of terms added together, only the fastest-growing one survives simplification, exactly like O(n² + n) simplifying down to O(n²).

items.prompt: Implement `needsDataStructureFix(hasNestedScan, dataSize)` — return `true` if there's a nested scan AND the data size is large enough to matter (`dataSize > 1000`), modeling when a quadratic pattern is actually worth fixing in practice.

nested scan, tiny data -> not urgent
no nested scan -> never needs this fix

items.prompt: Implement `expectedComplexityClass(usesHashLookup, hasOuterLoop)` — return `'O(n)'` if there's an outer loop with a hash lookup inside, `'O(n^2)'` if there's an outer loop with a scanning (non-hash) lookup inside, or `'O(1)'` if there's no outer loop at all.
items.explanation: This mirrors the exact before/after of the unit's incident: the outer loop alone sets a floor of O(n), and whether the inner lookup is hash-based or a scan decides whether that floor holds (O(n)) or multiplies into O(n²).

items.prompt: Implement `worstCaseForLookup(dataStructure)` — return the worst-case (not average-case) complexity of a membership check for `'array'` (always `'O(n)'`) or `'set'` (still `'O(n)'` in the rare pathological hash-collision case, not `'O(1)'`).
items.explanation: Both are O(n) in the worst case — this deliberately counters the common mistake the unit flags: a Set's O(1) is an average-case claim, and under pathological hash collisions its worst case degrades back to O(n), the same as a plain array scan.
